lesson_title: Non-Metals Make Acids, Metals Make Bases
hook_text: Your stomach and a car battery both run on strong acid. Here is how to spot an acid from its formula.
clip_script: Two strong acids run the school lab. Hydrochloric acid, HCl, is already inside you: your stomach makes it to digest food and kill germs, and hardware stores sell it as pool acid. Sulfuric acid, H2SO4, sits inside every car battery, and factories use mountains of it to make fertiliser. Concentrated, it pulls water out of sugar and leaves a tower of black carbon. Now the big pattern. Burn a non-metal like carbon or sulfur, dissolve the oxide in water, and you get an acid. That is why cooldrinks fizz and coal smoke makes acid rain. Burn a metal like magnesium and its oxide makes a base. Metal oxides, metal hydroxides and metal carbonates such as limestone are all bases. So read the formula: H in front, acid. A metal with O, OH or CO3, base.
visual_style: Split screen of a stomach diagram and a car battery; sugar foaming into black carbon; two columns sorting formulae into acid and base with a satisfying slide.
pacing: Quick two-acid intro, a dramatic sugar beat, then a steady sorting rhythm.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sort ten formulae into acids and bases.
